planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix; frost-tender and grown outdoors only in zones 10-11.

directions: This erubescens-complex climbing hybrid produces dark green leaves irregularly splashed with cream, white, and occasional pink sectors, carried on smooth green petioles that distinguish it from the similar but burgundy-stemmed 'White Knight.' Train it up a moss pole so maturing leaves size up and hold heavier variegation than trailing growth typically shows. Give strong, bright indirect light to sustain the white patterning, since low light pushes new growth back toward solid green, and trim away any all-white leaves that lack chlorophyll and cannot sustain themselves. Let the potting mix dry slightly between waterings and keep humidity high.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix; frost-tender and grown outdoors only in zones 10-11.

directions: Bred in Florida from a multi-species cross including P. wendlandii, hastatum, and erubescens, this self-heading, non-climbing hybrid forms a dense rosette of broad, elliptic leaves that emerge deep burgundy-red and darken toward near-black as they mature under bright light. It is one of the parents behind the larger hybrid 'Rojo Congo' and shares its compact, upright habit but stays smaller and even darker in color. Bright, indirect light deepens the near-black leaf tone, while low light shifts new growth toward a plainer reddish-green. Let the chunky mix dry slightly between waterings and feed lightly during the growing season.
sources: University of Florida Mid-Florida Research and Education Center

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in very well-drained, chunky aroid mix; frost-tender and grown outdoors only in zones 10-11.

directions: A cross between velvet-leaved P. verrucosum and P. melanochrysum, this vigorous climbing hybrid produces huge, quilted, deep olive-green leaves with a soft velvety sheen and pale contrasting veins, combining the bold size of melanochrysum with the more manageable vigor of verrucosum. Provide a moss pole or totem, since it climbs strongly and produces larger, more dramatically textured leaves when grown vertically rather than left to trail. Keep humidity high and let the top two to three inches of the chunky mix dry between waterings, since standing water quickly leads to root rot. Bright, indirect light keeps growth full; deep shade produces sparse, stretched leaves.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix; frost-tender and grown outdoors only in zones 10-11.

directions: Native from Mexico to Panama, this smaller climbing relative of Monstera deliciosa presses its young, glossy, dark green leaves flat against a support in an overlapping shingled pattern before shifting to the elongated, perforated adult foliage that develops once the vine reaches a mature climbing stage. Provide a rough totem, bark slab, or moss pole for the aerial roots to grip, since flat, close contact with a climbing surface is what triggers the juvenile shingling habit. Keep the mix evenly moist in active growth and slightly drier in winter, and maintain high humidity to prevent crisping leaf edges. Bright, indirect light produces the densest shingling; low light causes leaves to space out and stretch.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix; frost-tender and grown outdoors only in zones 10-11.

directions: Native to Costa Rica, this climbing species produces narrow, elongated leaves so heavily perforated at maturity that more of each blade is open space than solid tissue, an extreme fenestration pattern that gives rise to its Esqueleto (skeleton) trade name. Train it onto a moss pole or bark totem, since aerial-root contact with a climbing surface encourages larger, more deeply fenestrated adult leaves than a plant left to trail. Allow the chunky mix to dry out between thorough waterings, as this species is markedly less tolerant of soggy soil than Monstera deliciosa. Bright, indirect light and steady warmth with high humidity produce the fastest, most heavily perforated growth.

planting.note: Grow in bright, filtered light or morning sun in a large container of chunky, well-drained, organically rich mix; frost-tender and grown outdoors only in zones 10-11.

directions: This Mexican species is among the largest anthuriums grown, producing enormous, heart-shaped, ribbed leaves that can reach several feet long on a mature specimen, making it a bold architectural floor plant that needs generous floor space rather than a shelf or tabletop. It tolerates more direct morning sun than most thin-leaved anthuriums but still scorches quickly under harsh midday exposure, so filtered light or an east-facing position works best. Water when the top couple of inches of mix dry out, and avoid letting the pot sit in standing water. Feed lightly every few months with a phosphorus-leaning fertilizer to support its outsized leaf production.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained potting mix; frost-tender outside zones 10-11.

directions: A dwarf sport of common arrowhead vine, Mini Pixie stays only a few inches tall with small, soft pink-tinged, arrow-shaped juvenile leaves and a slow, compact growth rate that suits terrariums, dish gardens, and small shelf pots where a standard syngonium would quickly outgrow the space. Bright, indirect light keeps the foliage compact and brings out the strongest pink cast in new leaves, while low light causes leggier, more widely spaced growth. Water when the top inch of mix dries, and maintain moderate to high humidity for the neatest form. As with other syngoniums, the sap can irritate skin and is toxic if chewed by pets.
sources: African Violet Society of America (Violet Barn cultivar records)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained potting mix; frost-tender outside zones 10-11.

directions: Part of the same Exotic Angel cultivar group as 'Pink Allusion,' Berry Allusion produces arrow-shaped leaves washed in dusty berry-pink over a light green base with darker pink venation, forming a bushy, upright clump while young before sending out longer climbing stems with age. It suckers freely from the base, quickly filling out a pot with multiple growing points rather than staying a single stem. Moderate to bright indirect light brings out the deepest berry coloring, while low light shifts new growth toward plain green. Water when the topsoil dries and pinch growing tips to keep the plant bushy and compact.
